content: Let's not make such flippant remarks about pushing someone out of the community for their views. I have a lot of respect for Patrick's views on what Lean/Mathlib should aim towards, and I'm glad he can express his stronger level of skepticism towards vibe coding here.
(Aside: I'm keen to have everyone settle on the phrase "syntax programming", for what we all used to do. I can't really imagine wanting to type out all that generic python and CI code by hand!)
"Coding", when done properly and correctly is software engineering. Calling software engineering "syntax programming" is a very dismissive and condescending term to describe that.
I'd leave it to professional software engineers who have spent decades in this field or at least have a CS background of several years to converge on such terminology.

Kim Morrison said:

for what we all used to do

what and who does this refer to? i imagine there's enough people here that if the "who" refers to the author and the audience, the "what" can't be software engineering as there's people still doing that, and it can't be vibe coding because there's people who never had AI write code for them?

Shreyas Srinivas said:

"Coding", when done properly and correctly is software engineering. Calling software engineering "syntax programming" is a very dismissive and condescending term to describe that.

There is clearly a huge amount of coding that is not software engineering, I would bet that everyone in this thread has done that, and it is extremely practically and economically relevant!

If you said that "Making dinner, when done correctly, is cooking": sure, this is the higher standard for food preparation. But it is neither necessary nor even desirable that we should all cook every time we need to put dinner together. What would happen to all the world's leftover pizza that we no longer warm up! :)

Similarly, I regularly write one-off scripts or simple convenience utilities that won't live beyond a week -- or even a single python -cinvocation -- that do not need to be engineered.

I think there's a reasonable stance that (say) if you vibe code something, you should give it a bit extra review before sharing it with others. But you can't ignore that much code is already manually written to a standard far far below what an LLM outputs, and in this case the _quality_ at least does not pose a problem.

I think even for this perhaps less controversial (or perhaps not...) use case of code for CI that this has not been universally positive. I've become wary about merging such PRs too quickly when I see Claude is involved.

Alex Meiburg said:

Similarly, I regularly write one-off scripts or simple convenience utilities that won't live beyond a week -- or even a single python -cinvocation -- that do not need to be engineered.

CI lives longer than one week.

I think there's a reasonable stance that (say) if you vibe code something, you should give it a bit extra review before sharing it with others. But you can't ignore that much code is already manually written to a standard far far below what an LLM outputs, and in this case the _quality_ at least does not pose a problem.

  1. There is a big difference between that and calling something "syntax programming".
  2. "Much code is already manually written to a standard..." => Yes there are bad engineers. That doesn't justify ascribing superlative abilities to LLMs, and describing human authored work as "syntax programming".

Note that I am not opposed to using slop where it doesn't matter. If you prove an annoying but trivial lemma in lean with codex/claude, that's fine by me. I do that too. However CI is critical infrastructure. So I and many engineers would prefer hand written code to AI slop.

Yes there are bad engineers

This tells me that you've completely missed my point. There are many people who need to write code who are not engineers.

Lifeguards and kindergarten teachers aren't "bad doctors" even though they, respectively, save lives using medical treatment, and apply first aid kits for playground scrapes, regularly. Because they aren't doctors to begin with.

Again, I agree there is a point that things like CI have longer lifetimes and more room for downstream consequences, and that vibe coding is not welcome there.

But saying that "coding done correctly is software engineering" or that code of sub-LLM quality is because of "bad engineers" is simply objectively untrue; that is not what those words mean in English, and that is not how any industry in the real world that I'm aware of operates.

Even companies that you could say are "software engineering companies", e.g. Google, Microsoft, Meta... increasingly have a significant fraction of code in their codebase written by people who are not "software developers" or "software engineers" by title nor training nor in practice. They're product managers, designers, research scientists, UX researchers... and they write code and check it in. That's their job. And it's better code when an LLM helps, and that doesn't mean they're bad at their job.

They're product managers, designers, research scientists, UX researchers... and they write code and check it in. That's their job. And it's better code when an LLM helps, and that doesn't mean they're bad at their job.

Without writing a long-winded response, I think it is clear that some people simply disagree with the operational and/or ethical soundness of this approach, and in an open source context are free to minimize their personal interactions with AI-generated code.

My main objection is to attaching labels to such people such as “syntactic programmers”. Choosing to not deskill oneself and write quality code is not morally or technically equivalent to vibe coding. So while it is absolutely accurate and fair to call vibe coded stuff “slop” because of the quality issues with its output as well as moral issues such as deskilling of work, energy issues etc, it is not justified to label people who don’t use LLMs “syntactic programmers”.

An example of @Alex Meiburg 's point in stuff related to what we do here. I have time to time made illlustrations for courses I teach, for instance one on Markov chains. I enjoyed this and it helped. The first one I made was for linear ODEs in dimension two.

Yesterday, I used Google AI studio to vibe code in a few minutes an illustration of ODEs and eigenvalues. I am not even teaching my course - I did it partly so whoever is teaching can use it but mainly to illustrate to my colleagues that it is easy to add illustrations (this was in the context of some course changes that made it relevant).

No comment about what anyone calls things, but often the goal is to do something useful (and show others they can easily do useful things).
